newsitem.title: KENYA: Report shows horrific sexual abuse of Rwandan women.
newsitem.headline: Report shows horrific sexual abuse of Rwandan women.

text.p: A human rights report on Tuesday detailed horrifying sexual abuse of women by Rwandan Hutu troops and militia in the genocide of up to a million people in 1994.

The report by the U.S.-based Human Rights Watch and the International Federation of Human Rights Leagues included testimonies from women individually raped, gang-raped, raped with objects such as sharpened sticks or gun barrels, held in sexual slavery or sexually mutilated.

"These crimes were frequently part of a pattern in which Tutsi women were raped after they had witnessed the torture and killings of their relatives and the destruction and looting of their homes," it said.
The report called on the International Criminal Tribunal on Rwanda's genocide to investigate and prosecute rape and other gender-related crimes.

"According to witnesses, may women were killed immediately after being raped," it said. "Other women managed to survive, only to be told they were being allowed to live so they would 'die of sadness'.
"Often women were subjected to sexual slavery and held collectively by a militia group or were signed out by one militiaman...and held for personal sexual service," it said.
"These forced 'marriages', as this form of sexual slavery is often called in Rwanda, lasted for anywhere from a few days to the duration of the (three-month) genocide, and in some cases longer."

The report said the exact number of women raped in Rwanda between April and July 1994 would never be known but most were members of the Tutsi minority attacked as a means of destroying their ethnic group.
"Rape was a strategy," said Bernadette Muhimakazi, a Rwandan women's rights activist. "They chose to rape. There were no mistakes. During this genocide, everything was organised."
The testimonies included accounts of members of the army and presidential guard raping corpses and mutilation of sexual organs or features held to be characteristic of ethnic Tutsis.

The International Tribunal for Rwanda meets on Wednesday in the northern Tanzanian town of Arusha to consider a defence call for the release of one of three Rwandans accused with genocide and crimes against humanity during the mass slaughter in Rwanda.
The report urged Rwanda's government to ensure equal protection for women under law and called on the international community to address the needs of women attempting to rebuild their lives.

"The genocide in Rwanda left a population that is 70 percent female, and the stories told by survivors defy comprehension," said Dorothy Thomas, director of the Human Rights Watch Women's Rights Project.
"What is clear is Rwanda will only rebuild itself through these women, and the international community must do everything possible to help them deal effectively with the past," she said.
The report said many Rwandan women who had been raped did not dare to reveal publicly what had happened and those who had children after being raped were the most socially ostracised.
"Widows are without families, without houses, without money. We become crazy. We aggravate people with our problems. We are the living dead," it quoted one Rwandan woman victim as saying.
